meta.title: Who really said "Real knowledge is to know the extent of one's ignorance"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Credited to Confucius — and genuinely his in spirit. It paraphrases Analects 2.17, but the exact wording is a modern gloss found in no scholarly translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Real knowledge is to know the extent of one's ignorance'?
meta.ogDescription: Confucius said it in substance (Analects 2.17), but this catchy wording is a modern paraphrase no primary source pins down. An honest look at the provenance.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 551–479 BCE · Chinese philosopher and teacher, Spring and Autumn period
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Confucius and genuinely Confucian in spirit — it compresses a real passage in the Analects (Book II, ch. 17), where the Master tells his disciple Zi Lu that true knowledge is to know what you know and to admit what you do not. But the catchy English wording “Real knowledge is to know the extent of one’s ignorance” appears in no standard scholarly translation, and no primary source pins that exact phrasing.

source.heading: Where it really comes from

docMeta.dd: The Analects, Book II (Wei Zheng), ch. 17
Loose modern paraphrase of a real passage
Sayings 6th–5th c. BCE; compiled later by disciples

source.excerpt: You, shall I teach you what knowledge is? When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it — this is knowledge.
trail: The genuine source is Analects, Book II (Wei Zheng), ch. 17, where Confucius tells Zi Lu that knowledge is to hold what you know and admit what you do not — James Legge’s translation at ctext.org ↗.

Wikiquote ↗ lists the authentic “to know what you know and what you do not know” passage in its sourced section, but does not carry “Real knowledge is to know the extent of one’s ignorance” as a genuine Confucius line.
Popular quote databases and even academic blurbs (e.g. Columbia’s ICCCR ↗) print the paraphrase as if verbatim, without citing any passage of the Analects.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular one-liner is a paraphrase of this passage
source.excerptNote: James Legge’s translation of Analects 2.17 (Chinese: “知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也”). The popular one-liner — “Real knowledge is to know the extent of one’s ignorance” — is a compressed paraphrase of this idea, not a sentence Confucius is recorded as saying in any scholarly rendering.

source.rightsNote: The underlying Analects text is ancient and long in the public domain, as is James Legge’s 19th-century translation. The modern paraphrase “Real knowledge is to know the extent of one’s ignorance” has no identified author or copyright and is too short to protect.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: About Confucius
author.bio: Confucius (Kǒng Fūzǐ) was a teacher, editor and political thinker of the Spring and Autumn period whose ethics of virtue, ritual and reciprocity shaped East Asian civilization for two millennia. He wrote no books himself; his sayings survive as the Analects (Lunyu), compiled by disciples after his death. Because that text is a patchwork of remembered aphorisms, many lines later ‘quoted’ from him — including this one — are paraphrases rather than his exact words.

cite.sourceCitation: Confucius, The Analects, Book II (Wei Zheng), ch. 17, trans. James Legge (London, 1861): “When you know a thing, to hold that you know it… this is knowledge.” The wording “Real knowledge is to know the extent of one’s ignorance” is a modern paraphrase of no fixed source.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: The line has become shorthand for intellectual humility — the idea that wisdom begins with mapping the edges of what you don’t know. It sits comfortably beside Socrates’ “I know that I know nothing,” which is part of why it circulates so freely in classrooms, boardrooms and LinkedIn posts.

What Confucius actually said in Analects 2.17 is subtler and more practical: not to measure your ignorance, but to be honest about the boundary in each case — claim what you genuinely know, and openly concede what you don’t. The popular wording keeps the spirit while sharpening it into an aphorism the Master never quite phrased.
detailsBody: Ancient Chinese aphorisms rarely survive translation as fixed English sentences. Different translators — Legge, Arthur Waley, D. C. Lau — render 2.17 in noticeably different words, none of which match the popular epigram. That mismatch is the tell that a memorable quote-card line is a modern gloss rather than a direct citation.
Treating it as ‘attributed’ rather than ‘fabricated’ is the fair call: the thought is demonstrably Confucius’, even if the sentence is not his.
context.pull: Confucius taught the honesty; the epigram is ours.
